answer.rationale: Rolllback is excluded because the latest build contains a compliance-mandated security patch that must not be reverted. Read-replica routing is irrelevant here because the degradation is on the write path, where the primary is the only writer. Adding capacity and enabling circuit breakers are real mitigations but secondary in this moment: capacity won't instantly absorb a p99 that has already multiplied by 5x inside one region, and a circuit breaker would protect the dependency but would also drop legitimate customer writes at peak settlement time, which directly conflicts with the primary objective of preserving sustained availability without losing writes. The strongest available lever is a regional failover: shift traffic out of the degraded primary region to a healthy region, the same pattern recorded in memory_b2 where a regional failover during the March degradation restored latency within minutes and shifted traffic cleanly with error rates recovering fast. The archived memory is worth verifying because it is the only prior record that directly matches the current shape of the incident (regional, latency-bound, traffic-shift-based recovery), so confirming the source record sharpens confidence in the chosen move. The failover will be staged: first drain and shift a small fraction of write traffic to the secondary region while monitoring error rate and replication lag, then expand the shift if the leading indicators stay green, and hold the line at the current split if they do not. This preserves customer writes by relocating rather than rejecting them, respects the compliance constraint on the patched build, and leaves the rest of the catalog (rollback, read replicas, capacity, circuit breakers) available for the next decision window if the failover alone is insufficient.
